content: Poor treatment outcomes for tuberculosis (TB) and a diminished overall health-related quality of life have been documented. Research indicates that depression may independently elevate the risk of developing TB. Furthermore, several anti-TB medications are associated with adverse mental health effects, including depression, anxiety, and psychosis. These side effects may necessitate either temporary or permanent discontinuation of the offending drug and/or the initiation of adjunctive psychopharmacological treatments. Individuals with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) are at an increased risk of experiencing depression, anxiety, or psychosis. Additionally, alcohol use disorders significantly heighten the risk of developing TB. Psychological stress stemming from stigma and discrimination can exacerbate mental health conditions or trigger substance use disorders in affected individuals. Those with drug-resistant TB and/or co-infection with HIV are at an even higher risk of developing mental health conditions, including substance use disorders. Many TB patients, particularly those with drug-resistant TB, experience varying degrees of mental distress related to the illness, its treatment, complications, and TB-associated stigma. In some cases, this distress, while not always pathological, can be alleviated through preventive measures such as health education or by providing access to social and financial resources. However, in severe and persistent cases, the distress may lead to significant functional impairment or disability, such as an inability to work, study, or care for family members, interpersonal strain, and social withdrawal. In such instances, a diagnosis of a mental disorder may be warranted. People already living with mental health conditions may experience a worsening of their symptoms upon receiving a TB diagnosis. Chronic psychological distress can lead to sustained autonomic and neuroendocrine responses, which weaken the immune system and negatively influence health behaviors, potentially jeopardizing TB treatment outcomes. TB disproportionately affects socially vulnerable populations, and TB-related stigma can intersect with and amplify other social stigmas, such as those related to poverty, mental health conditions, HIV co-infection, substance use, incarceration, or reliance on social protection services. The challenges associated with TB diagnosis or treatment, such as loss of income, can further deteriorate an individual’s mental health. TB-related stigma and discrimination can have profound negative effects on the physical and mental health of individuals with drug-resistant TB and may even trigger mental health conditions in those without a prior history of such conditions. Prevention, early identification, monitoring, and treatment of mental health conditions and substance use disorders are critical to improving both mental health outcomes and TB treatment success. Mental health care should be integrated into TB services, as outlined in the End TB Strategy and the WHO Framework for Collaborative Action on Tuberculosis and Comorbidities. This integration involves identifying TB patients with comorbid mental health or substance use conditions and addressing their needs through referrals to existing mental health services or task-shifting to primary care health workers trained in mental health assessment and management. Key mental health conditions affecting TB patients include depression, anxiety, psychosis, substance use disorders, and suicidal behaviors. The diagnosis, course of illness, treatment, and stigma associated with TB increase the likelihood of these conditions. Ideally, all TB patients should be assessed for mental health conditions or substance use disorders before or at the start of TB treatment and during routine evaluations. However, mental health and substance use services remain largely inadequate in many countries, with treatment gaps for severe mental health conditions reaching up to 90% in some regions. Opportunistic identification of mental health conditions during TB care may be a practical use of existing resources. Health workers can initiate assessments when patients present with signs of mental disorders, using standardized screening tools that are widely available, easy to administer, and validated across diverse settings. Screening tools provide information on symptom severity rather than diagnostic status, helping to identify individuals in need of further assessment or to monitor symptom changes over time. Additionally, individuals completing anti-TB treatment should be assessed for mental health conditions or substance use disorders. Linking patients to mental health care is essential to prevent loss to follow-up during treatment or to ensure continuity of care after discharge from TB programs. Establishing referral pathways between TB and mental health services is a critical component of service integration. Task-sharing with primary health care providers has been shown to reduce treatment gaps and increase coverage for priority mental health conditions. WHO has developed guidelines and materials under the Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) to support the management of mental disorders in non-specialized primary care settings. Non-specialist health workers, such as those serving TB populations, can be trained to identify, assess, manage, and follow up on priority mental health conditions. Collaborative care models, which involve systematic identification of affected individuals, close monitoring of outcomes, and treatment by care managers trained in delivering brief educational, psychological, and social interventions, are promising approaches for providing integrated, evidence-based, person-centered mental health care in physical health care settings. The 2022 Framework for Collaborative Action on Tuberculosis and Comorbidities provides guidance on scaling up collaborative action on TB and comorbidities, complementing the clinical aspects outlined in this guidance. At the systems level, integrating mental health care into TB services requires actions across multiple domains, including involving individuals with lived experience in service planning, ensuring supportive policies and legislation, aligning health financing to incentivize integrated care, building the capacity of health workers, and designing service delivery models that consider care processes and organizational structures.
